title: The Battle of Fort Dearborn
premise: 6 April to 16 August 1812 in twelve stops: the killings at Hardscrabble, the order to leave, the march down the beach, the surrender, and the houses where the Kinzies and Mrs. Helm hid.

opening.text:
JAUNT: THE BATTLE OF FORT DEARBORN. Spring 1812, where the Chicago River meets Lake Michigan. This story begins with the fort. In the summer of 1803 Captain John Whistler's company marched in from Detroit and built it in logs: barracks round a small parade, 'Two blockhouses' and 'a double row of palisades'. It has stood for nine years. Since 1810 it has been commanded by Captain Nathan Heald, with fifty-four regular soldiers. Across the river lives John Kinzie, the trader who supplies the garrison, with his family and his clerks; his stepdaughter Margaret is married to the fort's lieutenant, Linai Helm. A handful of other families live along the banks: the Ouilmettes, the Burnses, and the hands at Charles Lee's farm. The nearest American post is Fort Wayne, far to the south-east; Detroit, where the general commands, is farther still. War with Britain is coming, and every report that reaches the fort makes it feel smaller and farther from help. 

Twelve stops in date order, with the time of day set for each. Long rides go Instantly; every place keeps its stop.

The situation is about to ignite, three miles up the river, a little before sunset on 6 April 1812.

stops.text: 6 April 1812, a little before sunset. Three miles up the river's South Branch is a farm called Lee's Place, later known as Hardscrabble. Charles Lee, who 'did not live on the premises, but occupied a house near the fort', owns it; it grows food the garrison buys. In the log house are Liberty White, who runs the farm, a discharged soldier, a Canadian hand and Lee's young son. Eleven armed men walk in and sit down. Captain Heald wrote ten days later that they were 'supposed to be Winnebagoes'. Sensing trouble, the soldier and the boy slip across the river, as if to fodder the cattle at the haystacks, and run. Behind them they hear two shots. White and the Canadian are killed. Downriver, a family with a day-old baby has no idea what is coming.

6 April, dusk. Running downriver toward the fort, the two pause opposite this house, where the Burns family live, and shout across to warn them. At the fort Ensign George Ronan, 'a young cadet direct from West Point', takes five or six soldiers upriver in a flat-bottomed scow and brings Mrs. Burns out, 'with her infant of scarcely a day old, upon her bed to the boat'. A corporal and six men are still upriver fishing, so 'the commanding officer ordered a cannon to be fired'. They row home in the dark past the silent farm, find a scalped body by touch, and reach the gate about eleven at night. Heald enrols fifteen townsmen as militia. For four months the settlement waits behind its guns. When the blow comes, it comes as a letter.

10 August 1812, morning, on the parade. The United States has been at war with Britain since June, and the British have taken Mackinac, the American post up the lake. General William Hull, commanding at Detroit, sends a runner, Winnemac, with a written order for Captain Heald: 'It is with regret I order the Evacuation of your Post owing to the want of Provisions'. The arms are to be destroyed, and the goods in the government store given away. Wau-Bun says the order 'was read next morning upon parade', and that the officers' 'unanimous advice was, to remain where they were, and fortify themselves as strongly as possible.' Heald chooses to obey. Outside the pickets, hundreds of people have already heard, and are gathering to see what Heald will promise them.

12 August, afternoon (Quaife thinks the 13th), on this open ground outside the pickets. Heald wrote that the Potawatomi of the country round 'came in from all quarters in order to receive the goods in the factory store'. He meets their leaders in council here and promises them the goods. His own officers will not come: 'Captain Heald alone attended on the part of the military.' Instead they take the blockhouses that overlook this esplanade, open the port-holes and point the cannon 'so as to command the whole assembly.' It is a council held under the guns. He has promised the goods. He has not said what he means to do with the guns and the whiskey.

13 August, early afternoon. This log building is the factory, the government's trading house. Out of it now goes everything on the shelves: 'blankets, broadcloths, calicoes, paints'. Heald adds 'a considerable quantity of provisions which we could not take away with us.' Hull's order said the goods could go to those 'desirous of Escorting you on to Fort Wayne'. What Heald keeps back, the guns, the powder and the whiskey, is what matters most to everyone watching. That night, inside the walls, Heald does something he hopes no one will notice.

13 August, evening, from above. A covered way runs from the fort's north-east corner down to the river. 'The same evening the ammunition and liquor were carried, part into the sally-port, and thrown into a well'. Muskets are broken up and dropped in after them. The rest of the liquor goes 'as secretly as possible through the northern gate, the heads of the barrels knocked in, and the contents poured into the river.' Heald feared they 'would make bad use of it'. It is not secret: the knocking carries, and 'the taste of the water the next morning was, as one expressed it, "strong grog."' By morning the river tastes of whiskey, and a rider from Fort Wayne is nearly at the gate.

14 August, sunset, at the main gate. Captain William Wells rides in from Fort Wayne with a Miami escort, Heald says 'about 30 Miamies'. Wells is Rebekah Heald's uncle; he has come to bring her and her husband out, but Wau-Bun says 'all too late'. That evening Black Partridge, a Potawatomi leader from the Illinois River, comes to Heald's quarters and hands back his peace medal: 'I will not wear a token of peace while I am compelled to act as an enemy.' It is the plainest warning anyone gives. At nine tomorrow the gate will open, and everyone inside will walk out of it.

15 August 1812, nine in the morning. 'On the 15th, at 9 o'clock in the morning, we commenced our march', Heald wrote. Out of the gate, down to the river's mouth here, and south along the beach: Wells and part of the Miami escort in front, then the fifty-four regulars, the wagons with the women and children, and the twelve townsmen of the militia. Wau-Bun says the band played the Dead March, and that Wells 'had blackened his face before leaving the garrison, in token of his impending fate.' The Kinzie family's boat, warned, waits at this river mouth. A mile and a half ahead, behind the sand bank, men are waiting.

About 9:40. The column walks with 'the lake on our left, and a high sand bank on our right'. 'We had proceeded about a mile and a half,' Heald wrote, 'when it was discovered that the Indians were prepared to attack us from behind the bank.' The soldiers charge up it. Behind them, at the wagons, Quaife writes, 'a deadlier combat, which we may perhaps think of as a separate battle,' is raging. The militia are 'cut down to a man'. Among the dead are 'Cicely, Mrs. Heald's negro serving-woman' and 'her infant son', two of the few people recorded as held in slavery at Chicago. Heald has a few dozen men left standing, and a decision to make.

About half past ten. Heald gathers his last men on 'a small elevation in the open prarie'. A Potawatomi leader called Black Bird comes out, shakes his hand and asks him to surrender, 'promising to spare the lives of all the prisoners.' Heald agrees. His count: 'twenty-six regulars and all the militia were killed in the action, with two women and twelve children.' Among them are Ensign Ronan, the young surgeon's mate Isaac Van Voorhis, and Captain Wells. Later Chicago remembered two cottonwoods near here as the place. The survivors are led back north, and at the Kinzie house the danger is not over.

15 August, sunset, at the house of John Kinzie, the trader who sold to the garrison. His family is spared and brought home under guard: 'At their own mansion the family of Mr. Kinzie were closely guarded by their Indian friends.' Mrs. Heald, badly wounded, is ransomed by Kinzie's clerk for a mule, and Kinzie takes a ball from her arm 'with his penknife.' Next day a war party from the Wabash, faces blackened, sit down silent in the parlor. Then Billy Caldwell, the Sauganash, walks in 'with a calm step' and greets them as friends; they ask only for 'some white cotton in which to wrap their dead'. A few doors west, a wounded woman is hiding, and men are searching the houses.

16 August, morning, while the fort burns. Margaret Helm, Kinzie's stepdaughter and Lieutenant Helm's wife, wounded at the wagons, has been brought here to Ouilmette's house by Black Partridge in 'the ordinary dress of a Frenchwoman of the country'. When searchers come, the family 'raised a large feather bed and placed her under the edge of it, upon the bedstead, with her face to the wall', and Mrs. Bisson sits sewing on the front of the bed. 'I can but die,' said she; 'let them put an end to my misery at once.' The searchers look round 'and left the house.' Quaife doubts the romance, not the rescue.

endings.text: 16 August 1812. 'The next morning, they set fire to the fort and left the place, taking the prisoners with them.' Only the brick magazine 'alone defied the fire'. On the third day the Kinzies were put into a boat for St. Joseph. Heald and his wife were taken there too, and the scattered prisoners were held in the villages 'until the following spring, when they were, for the most part, carried to Detroit and ransomed'. The army came back in 1816 and built the second Fort Dearborn on the same ground. Quaife's warning about Wau-Bun, the family's book that shaped this story for a century: its accounts do Heald 'grave injustice'.

keepsake.title: Captain Heald's report, Pittsburg, 23 October 1812
keepsake.text: 'I embrace this opportunity to render you an account of the garrison of Chicago.' The commander's own account of the evacuation, written ten weeks after it.

evidence.text: Captain Nathan Heald, writing from Chicago on 15 April 1812: 'On the 6th instant, a little before sunset, a party of eleven Indians, supposed to be Winnebagoes, came to Messrs. Russell and Lee's cabin, in a field on the Portage branch of the Chicago river, about three miles from the garrison, where they murdered two men, one by the name of Liberty White, an American, and the other a Canadian Frenchman whose name I do not know.' The 1895 editors add the name [Debou] in brackets.
evidence.locator: p. 43, data/research/books/text/moses_kirkland_history_of_chicago_v1.txt lines 6876-6890 (machine OCR of the 1895 printing, read as corrected: Heald's letter of 15 April 1812)

evidence.text: Wau-Bun dates the attack to the 7th and tells the escape. A discharged soldier and a boy (Lee's son, by ch. XIX) left the visitors in the cabin and walked to the two canoes tied by the bank. The soldier 'pointed to the cattle which were standing among the haystacks on the opposite bank, and made signs that they must go and fodder them'. Once across, hidden by the haystacks, 'they took to the woods' and made for the fort, hearing two shots behind them. Their story: the farm was 'occupied by a Mr. White and three persons employed by him'.
evidence.locator: ch. XVIII, Massacre at Chicago, Project Gutenberg eBook #12183 plain text, the April section; ch. XIX for the boy as Lee's son

evidence.text: Wau-Bun: running down the river the two fugitives 'arrived opposite Burns's, where, as before related, they called across to advertise the family of their danger, and then hastened on to the fort.' Ensign Ronan volunteered with five or six soldiers: 'They ascended the river in a scow, and took the mother, with her infant of scarcely a day old, upon her bed to the boat'. A corporal and six men were fishing upriver, so 'the commanding officer ordered a cannon to be fired, to warn them of danger.'
evidence.locator: ch. XVIII, Massacre at Chicago, Project Gutenberg eBook #12183 plain text, the April section

evidence.text: The two runners left the cabin after the visitors came, which Heald puts a little before sunset, and ran some three miles down the river, stopping opposite the Burns house on the way; this stop is set at dusk. The hour is not recorded.
evidence.reasoning: Heald's letter of 15 April 1812 gives the arrival at the cabin as a little before sunset and the distance as about three miles; Wau-Bun has the runners call across to Burns's on their way down to the fort. Nobody wrote down the hour of the warning, so dusk is the reading of those two facts, not a found time.

evidence.text: Quaife (1913): 'after the murders at the Lee farm, Captain Heald enrolled fifteen militiamen from the civilian population outside the fort.' Wau-Bun: the people outside the fort 'now intrenched themselves in the Agency House'; its piazzas 'were planked up, for greater security, port-holes were cut, and sentinels posted at night.'
evidence.locator: Quaife, the chapter on the first fort (Gutenberg #69274 plain text, the paragraph on the civilians around the fort); Wau-Bun ch. XVIII, Massacre at Chicago, Project Gutenberg eBook #12183 plain text

evidence.text: General William Hull's order, Sandwich, 29 July 1812, found among the Heald papers and first printed by Quaife: 'It is with regret I order the Evacuation of your Post owing to the want of Provisions only a neglect of the Commandant' ... 'You will therefore Destroy all arms & ammunition, but the Goods of the Factory you may give to the Friendly Indians who may be desirous of Escorting you on to Fort Wayne & to the Poor & needy of your Post.'
evidence.locator: note 583, Gutenberg #69274 plain text, the evacuation chapter

evidence.text: Heald's journal: 'On the 9th of Augt, 1812, rec'd orders from Genl Wm. Hull to evacuate the Post of Chicago and proceed with my Command to Detroit.' Quaife: 'The next day the Indian runner. Winnemac, delivered to Captain Heald at Fort Dearborn his order for the evacuation.' Wau-Bun puts the runner, Winnemeg or Catfish, a Potawatomi, at the post on the 7th, bringing despatches that 'announced the declaration of war between the United States and Great Britain'. Wau-Bun: 'The order for evacuating the post was read next morning upon parade', and the officers' 'unanimous advice was, to remain where they were, and fortify themselves as strongly as possible.' Quaife defends Heald: 'Obedience to orders is the primary duty of a soldier.'
evidence.locator: Quaife Appendix III (Heald's journal) and the evacuation chapter; Wau-Bun ch. XVIII, Massacre at Chicago, Project Gutenberg eBook #12183 plain text

evidence.text: Heald's report: 'The neighboring Indians got the information as early as I did, and came in from all quarters in order to receive the goods in the factory store, which they understood were to be given them.' His warriors on the 15th were 'mostly of the Potawatamie nation' (the Potawatomi, as the name is now written). Wau-Bun puts a council on the afternoon of the 12th: 'Captain Heald alone attended on the part of the military.' His officers 'took command of the block-houses which overlooked the esplanade on which the council was held, opened the port-holes, and pointed the cannon so as to command the whole assembly.' Quaife thinks the council was 'probably' on the 13th.
evidence.locator: Appendix IV, Captain Heald's official report, Pittsburg, 23 October 1812 (from Brannan, Official Military and Naval Letters, 1823, p. 84), Project Gutenberg eBook #69274 plain text; Quaife note 589 and the evacuation chapter; Wau-Bun ch. XVIII, Massacre at Chicago, Project Gutenberg eBook #12183 plain text

evidence.text: Heald's report: 'On the 14th, I delivered the Indians all the goods in the factory store, and a considerable quantity of provisions which we could not take away with us.' Wau-Bun, which dates it the 13th: 'the goods, consisting of blankets, broadcloths, calicoes, paints, etc., were distributed, as stipulated.'
evidence.locator: Appendix IV, Captain Heald's official report, Pittsburg, 23 October 1812 (from Brannan, Official Military and Naval Letters, 1823, p. 84), Project Gutenberg eBook #69274 plain text; Wau-Bun ch. XVIII, Massacre at Chicago, Project Gutenberg eBook #12183 plain text

evidence.text: Heald's report: 'The surplus arms and ammunition I thought proper to destroy, fearing they would make bad use of it if put in their possession. I also destroyed all the liquor on hand after they began to collect.' Wau-Bun: 'The same evening the ammunition and liquor were carried, part into the sally-port, and thrown into a well which had been dug there to supply the garrison with water in case of emergency; the remainder was transported as secretly as possible through the northern gate, the heads of the barrels knocked in, and the contents poured into the river.' The muskets 'were broken up and thrown into the well'. The noise betrayed it, and 'the taste of the water the next morning was, as one expressed it, "strong grog."'
evidence.locator: Appendix IV, Captain Heald's official report, Pittsburg, 23 October 1812 (from Brannan, Official Military and Naval Letters, 1823, p. 84), Project Gutenberg eBook #69274 plain text; Wau-Bun ch. XVIII, Massacre at Chicago, Project Gutenberg eBook #12183 plain text

evidence.text: Heald's report: 'On the 13th, Captain Wells, of Fort Wayne, arrived with about 30 Miamies, for the purpose of escorting us in, by the request of General Hull.' Wau-Bun has him arrive on the 14th 'with fifteen friendly Miamis' to save 'his relative, Captain Heald', and says he came 'all too late': the ammunition was already destroyed. Quaife: Heald's wife Rebekah was 'the niece of Captain Wells'.
evidence.locator: Appendix IV, Captain Heald's official report, Pittsburg, 23 October 1812 (from Brannan, Official Military and Naval Letters, 1823, p. 84), Project Gutenberg eBook #69274 plain text; Quaife, the evacuation chapter; Wau-Bun ch. XVIII, Massacre at Chicago, Project Gutenberg eBook #12183 plain text

evidence.text: Wau-Bun: on the evening after the second council 'Black Partridge, a conspicuous chief, entered the quarters of the commanding officer' and gave back his medal: 'I will not wear a token of peace while I am compelled to act as an enemy.' Quaife: Black Partridge was 'a Pottawatomie chief from the Illinois River' (a Potawatomi leader); of the two contemporary versions, Lieutenant Helm's and Sergeant Griffith's through McAfee, both record his warning and 'Helm alone mentions the surrender of the medal.'
evidence.locator: ch. XVIII, Massacre at Chicago, Project Gutenberg eBook #12183 plain text; Quaife, the evacuation chapter and note 591

evidence.text: Heald's report: 'On the 15th, at 9 o'clock in the morning, we commenced our march: a part of the Miamies were detached in front, and the remainder in our rear, as guards, under the direction of Captain Wells. The situation of the country rendered it necessary for us to take the beach, with the lake on our left, and a high sand bank on our right, at about 100 yards distance.' Wau-Bun: 'As the troops left the fort, the band struck up the Dead March', and Wells 'had blackened his face before leaving the garrison, in token of his impending fate.' Mrs. Kinzie's boat 'had scarcely reached the mouth of the river, which, it will be recollected, was here half a mile below the fort, when another messenger from To-pee-nee-bee arrived to detain them where they were.' Quaife lists the order: Wells and part of the Miamis, the garrison, the women and children, the twelve Chicago militia.
evidence.locator: Appendix IV, Captain Heald's official report, Pittsburg, 23 October 1812 (from Brannan, Official Military and Naval Letters, 1823, p. 84), Project Gutenberg eBook #69274 plain text; Quaife, the battle chapter; Wau-Bun ch. XIX, Narrative of the Massacre, Continued, Project Gutenberg eBook #12183 plain text

evidence.text: Heald's report: 'We had proceeded about a mile and a half, when it was discovered that the Indians were prepared to attack us from behind the bank. I immediately marched up with the company to the top of the bank, when the action commenced; after firing one round, we charged, and the Indians gave way in front and joined those on our flanks.' Quaife: 'Meanwhile a deadlier combat, which we may perhaps think of as a separate battle, was raging around the wagons in the rear.' The militia 'were cut down to a man'. Among the dead were 'Cicely, Mrs. Heald's negro serving-woman' and 'her infant son, who also perished', two of the few recorded people held in slavery at Chicago.
evidence.locator: Appendix IV, Captain Heald's official report, Pittsburg, 23 October 1812 (from Brannan, Official Military and Naval Letters, 1823, p. 84), Project Gutenberg eBook #69274 plain text; Quaife, the battle chapter and note 596

evidence.text: This stand is on the reconstructed 1812 beach at Heald's 'about a mile and a half', measured along the march from the fort site down the river and the shore.
evidence.reasoning: data/terrain/1812_evacuation_readings.json and the route tools/derive_evacuation_1812.py lays from it: the station 'About a mile and a half (Heald)' at local E 1318.0, N -1852.7, the middle of a band of 1.25 to 1.75 miles. The stand is 6 m inland of it. It is a reading of his distance, not a marked place, and the scene card 'Where the attack happened' says the same.

evidence.text: Heald's report: he 'took possession of a small elevation in the open prarie, out of shot of the bank or any other cover' and was met 'by one of the Potawatamie chiefs, called the Black Bird' (a Potawatomi leader), who 'requested me to surrender, promising to spare the lives of all the prisoners.' The toll he gives: 'twenty-six regulars and all the militia were killed in the action, with two women and twelve children. Ensign George Ronan and doctor Isaac V Van Voorhis of my company, with Captain Wells, of Fort Wayne, are, to my great sorrow, numbered among the dead.' The warriors numbered 'between four and five hundred', and their loss 'was about fifteen.' The report opens: 'I embrace this opportunity to render you an account of the garrison of Chicago.'
evidence.locator: Appendix IV, Captain Heald's official report, Pittsburg, 23 October 1812 (from Brannan, Official Military and Naval Letters, 1823, p. 84), Project Gutenberg eBook #69274 plain text

evidence.text: Wau-Bun: Mrs. Heald, badly wounded, was ransomed by Kinzie's clerk Chandonnai for a mule and the promise of whiskey and brought to the boat, and then to the house, where 'Mr. Kinzie then performed the operation himself, with his penknife.' 'At their own mansion the family of Mr. Kinzie were closely guarded by their Indian friends.' On the 16th 'Black Partridge, Wau-ban-see, and Kee-po-tah, with two other Indians' sat in the porch as sentinels. A party from the Wabash, who had 'blackened their faces', came into the parlor and 'seated themselves upon the floor in silence'. Then Billy Caldwell, the Sauganash, 'entered the parlor with a calm step', laid his rifle behind the door and greeted them as friends; 'thus taken by surprise', they 'said modestly that they came to beg of their friends some white cotton in which to wrap their dead before interring them.'
evidence.locator: ch. XIX, Narrative of the Massacre, Continued, Project Gutenberg eBook #12183 plain text

evidence.text: Wau-Bun: Black Partridge had Mrs. Helm put on 'the ordinary dress of a Frenchwoman of the country' and led her to Ouilmette's house. When the searchers came, the household 'raised a large feather bed and placed her under the edge of it, upon the bedstead, with her face to the wall', and Mrs. Bisson, the sister of Ouilmette's wife, 'seated herself with her sewing upon the front of the bed.' Nearly suffocating, Mrs. Helm begged to be given up: 'I can but die,' said she; 'let them put an end to my misery at once.' The searchers looked about the room 'and left the house.' Quaife (1913) warns that this part of Wau-Bun may be heightened: 'That Black Partridge saved Mrs. Helm is probably true, but that the affair possessed the romantic aspect which it has come to assume in the popular mind ... seems unlikely.' Her first name is in Kirkland (1893): 'Margaret Helm, wife of Lieutenant Helm, and step-daughter of old John Kinzie'.
evidence.locator: ch. XIX, Narrative of the Massacre, Continued, Project Gutenberg eBook #12183 plain text; Kirkland 1893, the opening chapter, footnote [A] (Gutenberg #59624 plain text, line 590); Quaife Appendix II, on Mrs. Helm's narrative

evidence.text: Heald's report: 'The next morning, they set fire to the fort and left the place, taking the prisoners with them.' Quaife: the magazine, 'a small structure made of brick', 'alone defied the fire'. Wau-Bun: 'On the third day after the battle, the family of Mr. Kinzie, with the clerks of the establishment, were put into a boat' for St. Joseph. The prisoners, Wau-Bun says, were dispersed among the villages 'until the following spring, when they were, for the most part, carried to Detroit and ransomed'; Mrs. Lee and her infant were taken to Black Partridge's village on the Au Sable, and Mrs. Burns 'with her infant, became the prisoner of a chief'. Heald's journal: 'On the 16th, that is the day after [the] action, Mrs. Heald & myself were taken to the St. Joseph River by our new Masters.' The army came back in 1816 and began the second fort on the same site (Quaife, the chapter on the second fort). Quaife on Wau-Bun as a whole: its accounts 'all proceed, directly or indirectly from a common source', and do Heald 'grave injustice'.
evidence.locator: Appendix IV, Captain Heald's official report, Pittsburg, 23 October 1812 (from Brannan, Official Military and Naval Letters, 1823, p. 84), Project Gutenberg eBook #69274 plain text; Quaife, the description of the fort and the evacuation chapter; Wau-Bun ch. XIX, Narrative of the Massacre, Continued, Project Gutenberg eBook #12183 plain text

evidence.text: Quaife (1913): Ensign George Ronan was 'a young cadet direct from West Point', ordered to Fort Dearborn in March 1811; Lieutenant Linai T. Helm came from Detroit at his own request, for 'his straitened financial circumstances and the cheaper cost of living at Fort Dearborn as compared with Detroit.' Surgeon's mate Isaac Van Voorhis, writing in October 1811: 'In my solitary walks I contemplate what a great and powerful republic will yet arise in this new world. Here, I say, will be the seat of millions yet unborn'. Quaife: 'The man who at the age of twenty-two could pen these lines'. Heald's report: 'Ensign George Ronan and Doctor Isaac V. Van Voorhis of my company, with Captain Wells of Fort Wayne' were killed; Helm was taken prisoner.
evidence.locator: Quaife, ch. VII, the paragraph beginning 'In March, 1811'; ch. X, the paragraph on Van Voorhis; Appendix IV, Heald's report

evidence.text: Quaife (1913): 'At half-past five o'clock on the morning of July 14, 1803, the troops set out from Detroit'; they 'reached the Chicago River at two o'clock on the afternoon of August 17'. The fort: 'The barracks and other structures for the accommodation of the garrison were built around the four sides of a quadrangle', with 'Two blockhouses' and 'a double row of palisades'. In April 1810 Captain John Whistler was moved to Detroit, and 'Captain Nathan Heald, who, in turn, succeeded Whistler at Fort Dearborn'. Heald's report: 'Our strength was fifty-four regulars and twelve militia'.
evidence.locator: Quaife 1913, the chapters on the building of the fort, the garrison of 1810 and the evacuation, Project Gutenberg eBook #69274 plain text

evidence.text: Wau-Bun (1856): 'On the north side of the main stream, but quite near its junction with Lake Michigan, stood (as has already been described) the dwelling-house and trading-establishment of Mr. Kinzie.' 'The fort was situated on the southern bank, directly opposite this mansion'. The Chicago Reader (2018): in January 1812 Heald made 'Messrs. Kinzie & Forsyth' the exclusive fort sutlers. Kirkland (1893): Margaret Helm was the 'step-daughter of old John Kinzie'.
evidence.locator: Wau-Bun, the April section; the Reader, the sutler paragraph; Kirkland, the Helm narrative

evidence.text: Currey (1912): 'Lee's place was also known as "Hardscrabble," a name which continued to be applied to that neighborhood for many decades thereafter.' The farm 'was owned by a man named Charles Lee, who, however, did not live on the premises, but occupied a house near the fort.' 'On the seventh of April of the fateful year 1812 the log house at Hardscrabble was occupied by three men and a boy. The man who seems to have been in charge of the work at the farm was one Liberty White, and with him were a discharged soldier, also a Frenchman named Debou, and the boy, a son of Mr. Lee's.' 'The products of the farm found a ready market at the fort'. Wau-Bun: 'Lee's Place, since known by the name of Hardscrabble, was a farm intersected by the Chicago River, about four miles from its mouth.'
evidence.locator: Currey, ch. on Lee's Place, Project Gutenberg plain text lines 1455-1540; Wau-Bun, ch. XVIII, Massacre at Chicago, Project Gutenberg eBook #12183 plain text

evidence.text: Currey (1912): that afternoon 'a party of soldiers from the fort, consisting of a corporal and six men, had obtained leave to go up the river to catch a supply of fish'. They passed Lee's place 'with the usual exchange of greetings' and fished two miles beyond 'until nearly dark. Suddenly they were startled by hearing the dull boom of a cannon'. Coming back, they found the place 'silent and deserted', stumbled on a body, and reached the fort 'about eleven o'clock at night'.
evidence.locator: Currey, ch. on Lee's Place, Project Gutenberg plain text lines 1455-1540

evidence.text: Quaife (1913): on 28 July 1812 'two Chippewa Indians reached Hull's camp at Sandwich bringing news of the surrender of Mackinac.' On 29 July Hull wrote, 'I shall immediately send an express to Fort Dearborn with orders to evacuate that post'. Hull was the American general commanding at Detroit.
evidence.locator: Quaife 1913, the chapters on the building of the fort, the garrison of 1810 and the evacuation, Project Gutenberg eBook #69274 plain text

evidence.text: Heald's journal has the order received on 9 August; Wau-Bun says it 'was read next morning upon parade'. This stop is set on the morning of 10 August, putting the two together; the hour is Wau-Bun's 'next morning', not a recorded time.
evidence.reasoning: Heald's own date for the order's arrival plus Wau-Bun's 'next morning' for its reading; the two sources differ by two days on the runner, so the date is a reading, not a record.

evidence.text: Wau-Bun puts the goods out on the 13th and the powder down the well 'The same evening', so the giving-out was by day; this stop is set at two in the afternoon of the 13th. No hour is recorded.
evidence.reasoning: Wau-Bun's sequence on the 13th (goods, then 'The same evening' the well); Heald dates the goods to the 14th. The hour is the jaunt's, inside the daylight the sequence needs.

evidence.text: Wells reached the fort on the 13th by Heald's report or the 14th by Wau-Bun; Black Partridge came to the commanding officer 'on the evening' after the second council. This stop is set at sunset on 14 August, the eve of the march.
evidence.reasoning: Wau-Bun's 'evening succeeding the council' and the march next morning; the hour is a reading of 'evening'.

evidence.text: The march began 'at 9 o'clock in the morning'; at a marching pace a column covers a mile and a half in about half an hour to forty minutes, so the attack at the bank is set at 9:40. Heald gives no hour for it.
evidence.reasoning: Heald's 9 o'clock start and his 'about a mile and a half', at an ordinary infantry pace of two to three miles an hour; an estimate, not a recorded time.

evidence.text: The fight at the bank, the struggle at the wagons and Heald's withdrawal to the rise all came before the surrender; this stop is set at half past ten that morning. No source gives the hour.
evidence.reasoning: Sequence in Heald's report (charge, withdrawal to 'a small elevation in the open prarie', parley, surrender) after a 9:40 attack; an estimate.

evidence.text: Two cottonwoods in the later Eighteenth Street were remembered as the place of the attack, a tradition written down from the 1880s; this scene stands them where it put them, and Heald's own mile and a half falls short of them.
evidence.reasoning: Heald's own distance against the later tradition; the stand follows the tradition and says so.

evidence.text: Wau-Bun has the Kinzies returned to their own house after the battle and Mrs. Heald brought there; this stop is set at sunset on 15 August. The Wabash party and Billy Caldwell came the next day. No hour is recorded.
evidence.reasoning: Wau-Bun's sequence: boat held at the river mouth during the fight, the family taken home after it; the hour is the jaunt's.

evidence.text: Wau-Bun sets the search of Ouilmette's house on the 16th, the day the fort was burned 'The next morning'; this stop is set at nine that morning. No hour is recorded.
evidence.reasoning: Heald's 'The next morning, they set fire to the fort' and Wau-Bun's placing of the search on the day after the battle; the hour is an estimate.
